highlights.title: API Separation & Prefetching
highlights.problem: Main-screen render time varied by user; for long-tenured accounts it sometimes took over 3 seconds.
highlights.analysis: Measured call time for each API used on the main screen and found the user info API was the slowest.
highlights.solution:
Designed a lightweight API with the backend team, selecting only the data needed for the main screen.
Shifted the heavy existing API to root-level rendering so it runs as background prefetching.
Refactored other pages that were also redundantly calling the same API.
highlights.result: Main screen load time: 3+ seconds → 0.6s. Pages with redundant calls refactored to near-zero or 0.3–0.4s.

highlights.title: E2E Testing & Reinforcement Learning Integration
highlights.problem: Some features required visual inspection, making automated testing impossible with existing methods.
highlights.solution:
Mock support made E2E testing feasible, so introduced E2E (Detox) and Jest.
Wrote test code focused on key features and components.
For tests requiring visual judgment, integrated a CNN model trained with reinforcement learning.
highlights.result: Automated tests for core features and components; reduced error occurrence rate.

highlights.title: Duplicate API Removal & Cache Management with Tanstack Query
highlights.problem: APIs fetching rarely-changing values on every focus event and APIs dependent on special states were causing dozens of redundant requests per session.
highlights.analysis: Profiled per-screen call patterns to identify APIs re-fetching rarely-changing values on every focus and those tied only to special states.
highlights.solution:
Configured Tanstack Query's stale time on the identified APIs to block unnecessary re-fetches.
After mutations, used query client to mark related data as stale so it refetches only when needed.
Removed complex useEffect-based state management code.
highlights.result: API calls per session: dozens → 3–4; improved state management productivity.

highlights.title: API Mock Testing Feature
highlights.problem: No way to arbitrarily change frontend UI state; test account limitations made diverse scenario testing impossible.
highlights.analysis: Analyzed API logs to rank endpoints by usage and selected the APIs accounting for 80% of call volume as mock targets.
highlights.solution:
Introduced API Mock Adaptor and implemented internal state control features for key app states.
Added mock coverage for the selected APIs.
highlights.result: Increased dev productivity and reduced bug occurrence rate compared to previous workflow.

highlights.title: Bundle Optimization
highlights.problem: Test code added to the project was being included in production builds, inflating bundle size.
highlights.solution:
Used babel.config and metro.config to automatically replace test-related source files with stub files at build time.
Removed console-related code and other production-unnecessary code.
Verified optimization results using atlas and hbc map to analyze bundle output.

highlights.title: Legacy Code Cleanup & Expo Migration
highlights.problem: Play Store 16kb page issue, legacy library conflicts, and duplicated functions/components were increasing development time.
highlights.solution:
Migrated Expo 52 → 54 to resolve the 16kb issue, removing unsupported libraries and fixing dependent code.
Extracted repeated logic from key files into shared functions, hooks, and components via refactoring.
highlights.result: Page-level source code reduced to 1/4; improved maintainability and readability.

highlights.title: Deployment Pipeline Setup
highlights.problem: Need arose to add automated testing to the deployment process and enable real-time OTA deployment, but no pipeline existed.
highlights.solution:
Added automated test scripts via npm commands and configured EAS build and deploy.
Added EAS channels for OTA updates and distributed an internal test app.
Configured internal test builds via babel.config and metro.config to include mock features in the bundle.
Built a 4-stage pipeline: local → internal test → final test → release.
highlights.result: Incident/bug response time: 2 days (iOS App Store review cycle) → 1 hour.

highlights.title: Server-driven UI for event banners and popups
highlights.problem: Changing the copy, imagery, or buttons of the home event banner and popup required a full app release. The event list API had no field for marketing content, and adding one meant a backend schema change with coordinated deploys — while the screen was already live, so nothing could alter how existing plain-text events rendered.
highlights.analysis:
Identified the existing free-form description column as a content carrier, which made server-driven UI possible with zero changes to the API contract.
Because that column already held plain-text descriptions and its contents are unvalidated external input, format classification and failure policy had to be settled before implementation.
highlights.solution:
Centralized a single function that classifies description into spec (JSON), text, or none, so banners and popups share the same interpretation.
Server-sent JSON is validated with zod — broken blocks are dropped individually, and unknown versions render only a fallback line.
Buttons keep only trusted URLs, and a close button is guaranteed so users can never get trapped in a popup.
Every new field is optional, so screens render exactly as before when the server omits them.
highlights.result:
Banner layout, popup blocks, button sets, and suppression windows became server-controlled without an app release, leaving both the event API schema and the legacy render path untouched.
A malformed block now degrades to that block disappearing rather than the card collapsing, and no server misconfiguration can trap a user inside the popup.
Added 96 event-related tests (93 across 9 new files, 3 in existing files); the full suite of 52 files and 622 tests passes.

aiHighlights.title: Designing and Operating a Multi-Agent Harness for Feature Implementation and Bug Analysis
aiHighlights.summary: Designed and operated two harnesses, Testing Harness and Feature Harness, using an orchestrator-designer skill built on Claude Code. Compared with a single-agent setup, it improved detection of boundary-condition defects and established a spec → implementation → verification pipeline.
aiHighlights.context:
When implementing features with a single agent, defects such as race conditions in screen transitions and state management occurred with some frequency.
In a multi-agent setup, cases of unexpected defects being identified were repeatedly observed.
There was a need to lock planning, implementation, and bug analysis into a fixed pipeline.
aiHighlights.approach:
Using a self-built orchestrator-designer skill on Claude Code, two harnesses were designed and operated.
The Testing Harness, which does not affect live features and is dedicated to bug analysis and cross-checking, was built first.
Then the Feature Harness was constructed for spec → design → simulation → conclusion → implementation → verification.
The Testing Harness was integrated into the verification stage of the Feature Harness, forming a single pipeline.
aiHighlights.verification:
By reviewing errors found during testing, the harness re-examined related areas and surfaced derivative defects.
Some of the harness's diagnoses were discarded or revised by a human.
As a result, a complex app-bootstrap component was decomposed into multiple hooks with clearer responsibilities, and related tests were added.
aiHighlights.impact:
Before and after adoption, personal metrics were measured at 5.17 → 9.25 commits/day (+79%) and 0.71 → 2.06 merged PRs/day (+190%).
The fix/feat ratio changed from 1.53 → 2.05, with no meaningful decrease confirmed.
Qualitatively, boundary-condition defects were caught more often, and reusable assets accumulated through documentation of the spec → implementation → verification flow.

aiHighlights.title: Building Jest Tests and Business Rule Documentation in Parallel
aiHighlights.summary: Built Jest unit and component tests alongside per-feature business rule documents with Claude Code. Established a system with 217 tests and 11 documents, where test failures function as a way to trace rule changes.
aiHighlights.context: The app lacked unit and component tests, so deployment stability needed to be improved. Adding tests was chosen as a way to secure quality without heavily modifying feature code. As the number of tests grew, it became harder to trace the relationship between rules and tests. The setup was expanded into a structure that manages business rule documents and a test catalog together.
aiHighlights.approach:
Claude Code was used as the primary tool.
Business rule extraction was handled by a human, test case candidate generation was done jointly by human and AI, and AI wrote the test code and per-feature documents.
Existing E2E tests and predefined types were provided as reference material to keep conventions consistent.
Instead of generating everything at once, tests were added sequentially by feature to keep each change reviewable.
aiHighlights.verification:
AI-written feature documents were reviewed first to confirm alignment with the rule definitions.
The implementation stage was handled by the Feature Harness, so the initial failure rate was low.
Afterward, the main type of failure came from existing tests breaking during code-structure changes.
As of now, there has been no confirmed case of tests proactively catching a production bug. A systematic way to validate test quality itself remains an open task.
aiHighlights.impact:
Starting from no test cases at all, the suite grew to 20 suites / 217 tests.
It consists of 11 feature documents and 21 test files.
Writing 5 new E2E tests used to take 1-2 weeks, but after introducing AI, roughly 200 tests were completed in 2 weeks.
By fixing business rules as document-test pairs, it became possible to secure stability through verification during new feature development and refactoring.

highlights.title: Introduced vendor raw data layer
highlights.problem: Each crawler always collected its target data directly from external sources, so data overlapping across crawlers was fetched multiple times.
highlights.analysis: Analyzed what the crawled datasets had in common and defined the collection pools that needed to be covered.
highlights.solution:
Created a raw_data schema and added dedicated crawlers for each collection pool.
Converted the existing collection crawlers to copy the data gathered by the raw_data crawlers.
Since some data may fall outside the defined pools and the raw crawlers themselves can fail, kept the existing collection code as a fallback path.
highlights.result:
Reduced duplicate collection cut API costs and token usage. In particular, even as new collection tasks are added, API costs and token usage stay fixed at current levels.
Fewer requests per minute also lowered the error rate.

highlights.title: Handled KR exchange-code reshuffle
highlights.problem:
EODHD's KR exchange-code reshuffle (legacy KS → split KO/KQ) left KOSPI stocks duplicated as ghost copies under KOSDAQ.
The price table's unique key was only (stock_id, date), so later-loaded ghost prices overwrote real KOSPI prices.
highlights.analysis: Monitoring showed the number of collected symbols dropped sharply, so checked the collected symbols in the DB and found only around 20 KOSDAQ (KQ) symbols were being collected.
highlights.solution:
Reported the issue to EODHD support with a concrete case and reproduction steps.
EODHD confirmed the error, fixed it, and replied by email.
highlights.result: EODHD completed correcting the faulty data, and the contaminated rows remaining in our DB were removed.

highlights.title: Diagnosed and Fixed a MySQL Buffer Pool Bottleneck
highlights.problem: A job that checked and replaced every row one by one took 4 hours. The server had 1TB of RAM, yet MySQL's buffer pool was still at its 128MB default.
highlights.analysis:
Drew up several hypotheses; since the job rewrote every row, an undersized buffer pool forcing repeated disk reads was the prime suspect.
Kept partitioning and index redesign as the fallback in case more memory didn't help.
Checked memory usage of the processes already running on the server with free -h.
highlights.solution: Sized the buffer pool conservatively at 16GB — about 1–2% of total RAM — since the server was shared with experiment workloads.
highlights.result: Cut the job from 4 hours to 30 minutes, without resorting to partitioning or re-indexing.

aiHighlights.title: Re-architected a legacy crawler codebase via a multi-agent orchestrator (/restructure)
aiHighlights.summary: Built a 9-agent custom pipeline that restructured a flat crawler codebase into a hexagonal-lite architecture with zero regressions.
aiHighlights.context: Refactoring a ~5,600-LOC, 27-file flat codebase in a single context was risky: with no domain boundaries, regression risk and verification overhead were high. A staged, verifiable multi-agent pipeline was needed.
aiHighlights.approach:
Built nine custom agents — structure audit, data-flow mapping, domain classification, structure design/cross-review, migration planning, step execution, and regression validation — plus a /restructure command.
Ran it as Discovery → Design (cross-reviewed) → approval → Migration Plan → approval → atomic step-by-step execution.
aiHighlights.verification: Each step ran in an isolated git worktree and had to pass a four-way regression check — pytest, AST diff, byte-equal, and import-graph — before merging. Critical legacy logic was preserved byte-equal in a separate module.
aiHighlights.impact: Completed 47 migration steps and 29 unit-level refactors with no regressions, and locked in 257 characterization tests. Restructured from 27 files into a 68-file, three-layer infra / shared / jobs architecture.

aiHighlights.title: Auto-Generated Characterization Test Campaign
aiHighlights.summary: Ran a 27-unit refactoring campaign (units 001–027) in which an AI agent generated characterization tests to pin existing behavior before each change.
aiHighlights.context: The legacy crawlers had no tests, leaving no safety net for credential removal, deferred engine initialization, or dedup consolidation.
aiHighlights.approach:
Equipped the refactoring orchestrator with a characterization-test writer (CharTestWriter) plus safety-net, dry-run, and spec modes, iterating a pin-tests → change → verify cycle per file-scoped unit.
Restricted all test runs to a safe_env with fake credentials so no real DB or API was ever touched.
aiHighlights.verification: Each unit's commit ships with a corresponding test file (33 tests/test_*_unit_0NN.py files, 267 test functions); pre-refactor pin tests judged not worth keeping were pruned by human review, with CharTestWriter hardened in the same pass.
aiHighlights.impact:
The resulting test suite became the regression baseline for the subsequent 50-step restructure and the round-3 dedup pass.
No quantitative effect beyond the test-asset count was measured.

highlights.title: Built a unified data-collection health-check framework
highlights.problem: Reviewed the monitoring queries and found they only checked for missing symbol counts.
highlights.analysis:
Analyzed several days of per-symbol row-count trends and confirmed that partial data gaps went undetected.
Also found some queries were written without the indexes in mind, making monitoring slow.
highlights.solution:
Abstracted gap detection into three layers (symbol presence, per-symbol row count vs. baseline, table-level distinct symbol count vs. baseline) with a runner, snapshot verifier, and cumulative baseline split into modules.
Consolidated 11 check items under a single registry, removing boilerplate for new ones.
Unified all statuses into one alert message and split the price section into US / KR.
Rewrote the slow queries with the indexes in mind.
highlights.result: Chunk-level gap detection rose from 0–1 to 3–4 per week. Heaviest price health check dropped ~50s → ~2s (~25× faster). Scattered alerts consolidated into one message, surfacing 11 statuses on a single screen within ~90s.

highlights.title: Isolated scheduler registration to eliminate full outages
highlights.problem: A bad schedule entry — invalid cron expression or missing handler — would raise during reload and abort the whole loop, halting every other job.
highlights.solution:
Wrapped the schedule rebuild loop with per-schedule try/except so one failure no longer aborts the entire reload.
Added a dedicated smoke-test job exercising the registration / execution path on a regular cadence.
highlights.result: Full-scheduler outages caused by a single bad schedule no longer occur.

highlights.title: Deployment process automation
highlights.problem: Every release required repeating the deployment manually, which was slow and left room for human error such as skipped steps.
highlights.solution:
Consolidated a multi-step deployment process into a single automated command.
Added automatic pre-deployment checks to block faulty releases caused by missing or wrong settings.
Standardized the process so every release runs the same way, removing repetitive manual work.
highlights.result: Manual deployments of ~10 minutes now complete automatically in ~10 seconds, removing repetitive manual work and the associated risk of error.

highlights.title: SSR/CSR split with a rollup-first cache
highlights.problem:
Verdicts had to be recomputed against a 170M-row, 29GB vintage price table that re-ingests full history under a new filing_date every day. Three query classes blew past the 25s statement ceiling, and two freshness columns had no index at all (13.1s and 4.7s). Dashboard traffic risked starving the crawl jobs sharing the same server.
The initial implementation ran all of these heavy queries during SSR before returning HTML, blocking the entire first paint until every query finished.
highlights.analysis: Benchmarked 19 queries directly against the server before writing the app, recording row counts, table sizes, index coverage and latency. Index position on the freshness column proved to be the only variable driving cost — and it can be detected from information_schema at boot.
highlights.solution:
Split rendering into two paths: SSR returns the first HTML from cached local SQLite only, while monitoring queries against the collection DB moved to the client (CSR) after the page loads.
Persisted every verdict to a local SQLite rollup; the dashboard reads the rollup first and recomputes only what is past TTL.
Split TTL into two tiers — 300s for indexed tasks, 6h for unindexed ones.
Capped the pool at 4 connections and re-applied MAX_EXECUTION_TIME on every checkout, since pooled connections carry prior session state.
Pushed every aggregation over 25s to a nightly warmer and served all exploration screens entirely from local SQLite.
highlights.result: Cut dashboard load from 46.6s cold to 117ms warm (measurement recorded in the project README). Trend charts, heatmaps and sparklines no longer touch MySQL, so filter interaction adds zero load to the collection server.

highlights.title: Coverage for the raw-ingestion blind spot
highlights.problem: After the vendor read-through migration, the raw schema became the only place calling vendor APIs — but the existing monitoring bot only watched the curated schema. Curated jobs run in copy mode, so when raw stalls they silently re-copy yesterday's data and exit 0. Logs looked clean and no alert ever fired.
highlights.analysis:
Raw tables are append-only, so curated thresholds do not transfer: KR daily bars swing between 2,065 and 3,888 symbols a day and one copy job writes 4 rows on a normal day. Gating on symbol count would have flagged half of all healthy days. Cron runs Mon–Sat, so measuring lag in calendar days would turn every Monday red.
Also measured read costs up front: freshness MAX reads take 4–7ms while vintage DISTINCT aggregations take 7.8s — a four-order-of-magnitude gap.
highlights.solution:
Declared 9 raw jobs in a registry and built a separate verdict path treating freshness as the primary signal and row count as secondary.
Measured lag as missed runs excluding Sundays rather than elapsed days — one miss warns, two or more fails.
Built a reconciliation table pairing raw and curated freshness maxima, surfacing copy-only operation as a distinct state.
Classified dates preceding a table's first ingestion as indeterminate rather than failed, so the pre-migration window is not recorded as one long incident.
Kept only the light freshness reads on the request path and deferred vintage aggregations to the warmer — the inverse of the curated caching strategy, documented inline with the measurements behind it.
highlights.result: Surfaced two defects the existing alerting had never reported: a KR financials raw job stalled since 2026-07-27, and an S&P500 raw job collecting only 501 of 503 symbols. For the latter, traced the ticker-notation mismatch to both the producer (requesting dash notation) and the consumer (assuming dot notation) and wrote up a one-line fix.

highlights.title: Automated upstream drift detection
highlights.problem: Task definitions live in a monitoring-bot repo and raw job definitions in a crawler repo — both outside this repository. Hand-copying them means a newly added upstream task leaves the dashboard quietly showing all-green, and in a monitoring tool that failure mode never raises an alert.
highlights.solution:
Wrote an extractor that parses registry.py via ast instead of importing it, so it runs without any of the bot's runtime dependencies.
Stored the source sha256 alongside the output; a --check mode exits 1 on hash mismatch and prints exactly which tasks were added or removed.
Raw jobs have no upstream declaration to extract, so added a second check that walks the crawler job tree, matches raw table references against the hand-written registry, and verifies that the source paths quoted in the UI's rerun commands actually exist.
Reused the extracted table and column lists as the SQL identifier allowlist, so definitions and the query builder share one source of truth.
Where the upstream repo is absent, the check passes but prints that verification did not happen — distinguishing a passing check from a skipped one.
highlights.result: Any drift across 11 tasks and 9 raw jobs surfaces from a single command. The Docker build re-extracts when the upstream source is mounted, eliminating image-to-upstream divergence.

highlights.title: Cross-platform NAS container delivery
highlights.problem: The deployment target is an internal NAS operated only through a GUI. Building on an Apple Silicon machine yields an arm64 image, and native modules like better-sqlite3 keep the container from even starting on the x86 NAS.
highlights.solution:
Wrote a build script that cross-builds an x86 image via buildx, exports it to a tar, and prints the resulting architecture immediately so a wrong-arch image never reaches the NAS.
Used Next.js standalone output so the image runs without node_modules, and kept credentials and the local SQLite file out of the image.
highlights.result: Deployment reduced to entering port, volume and DB credentials in a GUI form. The verdict-history volume survives container deletion, and SQLite migrations run automatically at startup.

aiHighlights.title: Validating AI-drafted plans against measurement
aiHighlights.summary: Produced structured planning artifacts first, then measured the target database directly and explicitly discarded every premise the measurements contradicted before writing implementation code.
aiHighlights.context: The monitored database is an internal collection server with no schema documentation, so planning had to assume table structure, scale and indexing. Implementing those assumptions unchecked would have built the entire verdict engine on a false foundation.
aiHighlights.approach:
Fixed product definition, screens and data contracts as JSON planning artifacts up front.
Measured table existence, row counts, sizes, freshness-column indexing and query latency using read-only queries before implementation, recording results in a separate facts document.
Compared measurements against planning premises and recorded each contradiction in the docs before revising the design.
aiHighlights.verification: Confirmed that what the plan assumed to be a 500-symbol S&P500 universe is actually a top-71 universe, invalidating that premise throughout. Conversely, the v2 premise that vintage point-in-time data was impossible turned out to be false for price tables, reversing that decision. The v2 recollection-queue module was never built and is documented as unimplemented.
aiHighlights.impact: Implementation started with existence and indexing confirmed for all 19 target tables. No measurement was taken of how much development time this saved.
